title: The Map Room: Answering Geographic Questions by Hand
text:
Ask a geographic information system (GIS) how much of a county’s good farmland is still under forest, and it answers in seconds. It lays a map of what the land can support over a map of what the land is used for, keeps the places where good land and forest overlap, and adds up their area.
Before computers, people answered the same question by hand, in map rooms. They lined up the two paper maps, traced one onto film, and laid it over the other on a glass table lit from below. Then they measured every patch where the two overlapped, with a wheeled instrument called a planimeter or by counting dots on a transparent grid. The work was careful and slow, and it answered one question at a time. A question about cropland instead of forest meant starting most of the work over.
The map room is where this series, The Shape-Files, begins, because the first geographic information systems were built to take over that work.
The hand method lasted long after those systems arrived. In 1979, as they had every year for three decades, crews from the US Forest Service’s Pacific Northwest Region flew over the national forests of Oregon and Washington. They drew the damage from insects and disease onto paper maps, one outlined patch at a time. Back in the office, staff measured each patch by hand, with a planimeter or a dot grid, and added up the acres inside every reporting area and every landowner’s property (Fig. 1).1,2
The 1979 survey shows what this work looked like in practice. To follow the same process step by step, take an invented test area 12 by 8 km. Its two maps are drawn on sheets 24 by 16 cm at a scale of 1:50,000, where 1 cm on the map stands for 500 m on the ground. One map, a capability map, rates the land from class 1 (best for farming) to class 7 (worst). The other shows what the land is used for. The answer lies only where class 1–2 land on the first map falls under forest on the second. Because the test area is invented, the true answer is known, and the hand method can be checked against it.
Done by hand, the work came in four jobs: make the sheets agree, lay one over the other, measure each patch, and add up the patches.

title: The Map Room: Answering Geographic Questions by Hand
text:
First, make the sheets agree
Two maps can be compared only if they share a scale and the same sheet edges. In Canada, the standard topographic sheets are drawn at 1:50,000, the same scale as the test sheets,3 and it takes 13,150 of them to cover the country.4 Maps from different offices didn’t always match, so the first job was often redrawing one to fit the other.
Even matching sheets didn’t stay matched, because paper swells in damp air and shrinks in dry air. As early as 1928, the US Geological Survey (USGS) told its field surveyors to fix their sheets to the plane table, a drawing board on a tripod, “by brass thumbscrews or tacks, to reduce to a minimum the expansion or contraction caused by changes in climatic conditions.”5 Printers fought the same problem. Erwin Raisz, a cartographer at Harvard, explained in his textbook that each color of a map was drawn on its own sheet, “usually made on vellum because it does not change its shape and size with humidity.” Each drawing, he added, “must have register marks for perfect overprint,” so that every color printed in exactly the right place.6
Lining sheets up this way is called registration. Laying many sheets side by side raised a second issue. The same USGS instructions noted that neighboring sheets would in theory leave “small gores,” thin gaps, between rows laid edge to edge.5 Each sheet uses a map projection, a way of drawing part of the curved Earth on a flat surface, so neighboring sheets can never fit together perfectly. The instructions said the paper’s stretch was the bigger of the two errors, and the test area fits on a single sheet, so here only the stretch matters.

title: The Map Room: Answering Geographic Questions by Hand
section: Then, lay one over the other
text:
Then, lay one over the other
Seeing one sheet through another took a table lit from below. When the draftsman Eric Tallis joined the drawing office of Britain’s Geological Survey in 1946, the office’s light box “contained about 30 tungsten lamps and in use became hot enough to fry an egg.”7 Raisz’s 1948 textbook describes a smaller version, an 8-by-10-inch pane of thick glass set into a drawing table with a lamp underneath, “a simpler arrangement than the large tracing table with a glass top and a number of lamps.” “Copying maps and drawing color overlays,” a caption in his book says, “is best done over the transparent table.”6
On the test sheets, that means tracing the class 1–2 land from the capability map onto translucent film, laying the film over the land-use map on the lit glass, and outlining every patch where good land and forest coincide (Fig. 2). There are two such patches.


Fig. 2In about 1994, a Forest Service technician in Portland, Oregon, traces a paper map onto film over a light table to prepare it for digitizing. The lamp underneath makes the map’s lines show through the film.Photo: Julie Johnson, USDA Forest Service, Region 6 · Public domain · Flickr

Each tracing was another copy of the lines, and another chance for them to slip out of register.

title: The Map Room: Answering Geographic Questions by Hand
text:
Then, measure every patch
Turning an outline, however careful, into a number took an instrument that dated from the 1850s. The Swiss mathematician Jakob Amsler designed the polar planimeter in 1854 and described it in print in 1856.8,9 It has two arms, hinged together (Fig. 3). One ends in the pole, a weighted point pressed into the paper. The other carries a small measuring wheel and ends in a tracing point. The technician set the tracing point on the outline, read the wheel, traced the outline clockwise back to the start, and read the wheel again. The difference between the two readings gave the area on the map, and a constant for the map’s scale turned it into acres or hectares.10


Fig. 3A polar planimeter made in Germany for the American instrument maker Keuffel & Esser. The weighted pole arm (top) pivots on the tracing arm (middle), which carries the measuring wheel and dials; the bar below checks the reading against a known area.Photo: Central Intelligence Agency · U.S. government work · Flickr · cropped

The wheel does the measuring. It turns only when the tracing arm moves sideways, at right angles to its own length. With the pole outside the outline, the net turning of the wheel over one complete tracing, multiplied by the arm’s length, gives the area enclosed.11 Green’s theorem, a result from calculus that ties the area inside a loop to measurements taken along its edge, explains why. The same theorem is behind the shoelace formula, which a GIS uses to compute the area of a polygon, a shape stored as a list of corners.
The smaller the patch, the less accurate the planimeter was. Tests reported in a 1903 manual put its average error at about 0.08% on a figure of 200 cm² and about 2.6% on one of 5 cm².10 A good reading also depended on the person and the paper. A geographer at the State University of Iowa who was arguing for dot grids put it this way: the reading “will be accurate if the operator has a very steady hand and traces the boundary with utmost care, and if the surface of the map is neither too smooth nor too rough.”12 Forest Service guidance was to trace each patch at least twice and average the readings.13
Counting was the alternative. A transparent sheet ruled into small squares turned area into a tally, but the technician had to judge every square the boundary cut through, and the results drifted. With squares, the same Iowa geographer warned, “the same area measured on successive days by the same operator may appear to have either grown or shrunk in the meantime.”12 A grid of dots removed most of that judgment. Each dot stood for a fixed area at the map’s scale, and the technician counted the dots inside the outline. In a Forest Service test, dots were off by 1.84% on average and squares by 4.50%, and counting dots took two-thirds as long as counting squares.14
The Forest Service printed its dot grids on transparent cards, like the one from its Pacific Northwest station in Fig. 4, with grids of 16 and 64 dots per square inch and a table of acres per dot at eight map scales.15 The more dots that fell inside a patch, the more reliable the estimate. Two cartographers later estimated that a count of about 100 dots inside a patch has a standard error, the typical size of its miss, of roughly 1.5% of the area. Their example of a job the method suited was measuring “the total area of woodland shown on a map.”16


Fig. 4Timber Survey Aid No. 6, a Forest Service card of square and dot grids with a table of acres per dot. At 1:63,360, where an inch is a mile, each dot of the 64-dot grid stands for 10 acres.Card: U.S. Forest Service, Pacific Northwest Forest and Range Experiment Station, undated · Public domain · Flickr

At the test sheets’ scale, each dot on a grid of 16 dots per square inch stands for about 10.1 hectares (ha; a hectare is 10,000 m², about 2.5 acres) on the ground, and the two patches of good land under forest hold about 107 dots (Fig. 5). Counting by computer, with the grid placed at 200 random positions, shows how far a single count can miss:

The finer grid means four times as many dots to count, and in return nine counts in ten come within 2% of the true answer, 1,079.3 ha. These are ideal counts, with no tracing error and no tired eyes, and the boundaries in the test area are straight lines. Real boundaries curve and wander, and a Canadian Forestry Service study found that a count’s error depends on a patch’s shape as well as on how many dots fall inside it.17

title: The Map Room: Answering Geographic Questions by Hand
section: Finally, add it up, and start again
text:
Finally, add it up, and start again
The last job was arithmetic: add up the patches for each county or district, sheet by sheet. The Forest Service totaled its damage the same way, by reporting area.2
Done carefully, all of this produced a good answer, but only to the question that was asked. Ask how much class 1–2 land is under cropland instead, and the traced outline of the good land can be reused, but the overlap is new: 1,031.2 ha in three patches, each needing its own outline and its own count. Ask about class 3–4 land under pasture, 937.0 ha in four patches, and even the tracing has to be done again. The registered sheets were the only part of the job that every question could share.

title: The Map Room: Answering Geographic Questions by Hand
text:
A country’s worth of sheets
The test area shows the problem on a single sheet. The Canada Land Inventory faced it across a whole country. Approved by the federal government in October 1963, the Canada Land Inventory set out to map about 2.6 million km² (a million square miles). It recorded how the land was used and what it could support for agriculture, forestry, recreation, and wildlife.18,19 Its land-use mappers worked on those same 1:50,000 sheets wherever they existed. Elsewhere, they took whatever base they could find, from about 1:40,000 to 1:63,360, rescaled it photographically to 1:50,000, and traced it onto blank sheets of drafting film “prepared to a master grid.”20
The inventory planned on a computer from the outset. Roger Tomlinson, its data processing coordinator, put the start of the system’s design in 1963.19 The inventory’s program report later explained why: “Conventional methods of map compilation, area measurement and comparison between maps and statistical tables, would have imposed severe restrictions on the inventory program.”18 When Tomlinson described the inventory’s “geo-information system” in 1967, he defined the system’s central task by the hand method it was replacing. Overlay was “the well-known function of putting one map over another and examining the resultant data relationships,” and, “as with the manual method of overlaying maps,” the maps had to be “at a common scale and frame size.” The computer still needed every map traced by hand, but only once. After that, the overlays and the measuring were its job.19
Computers didn’t empty the map rooms quickly. Sixteen years after the inventory’s decision, the Forest Service crews behind Fig. 1 were still measuring by hand. The Pacific Northwest Region kept measuring by hand until 1988, when it got access to a GIS called the Map Overlay and Statistical System.1

title: The Map Room: Answering Geographic Questions by Hand
text:
Where it shows up today
In a GIS, the same four jobs remain, done by software under new names. Making the sheets agree is now the job of coordinate reference systems, which tie coordinates to places on the Earth, and of the conversions between them. In QGIS, a free desktop GIS, each map is a layer of stored shapes, and laying one over another is a single run of the Intersection tool, which “extracts the portions of features from the input layer that overlap features in the overlay layer.”21 The software computes each patch’s area from its corners, using the same mathematics as the planimeter, and adds up the county totals in one more step. Because the outlines are stored, the cropland question is one more run of the same tool on the same two layers, not a new tracing and a new count.
The Forest Service’s old survey maps went into the GIS too. As each one was digitized, the region replaced the totals its staff had counted by hand with totals computed from the stored outlines.1 The maps no longer had to be traced and measured again for every new question. Their geography was stored, ready to be overlaid, measured, and counted whenever the next question came along.

title: About The Shape-Files
text:
The Shape-Files tells the story of how geography became something computers can store, search and reason about. It starts in the map rooms where people answered questions with tracing paper and a ruler, and follows the thread through the first computer systems of the 1960s, the databases and workstations that came after, desktop GIS and open-source software, all the way to cloud-native data and the AI agents that work with maps today.

A new file comes out every week. Each one takes a single idea, format, algorithm or system and shows where it came from and how it works. The history is told with diagrams and worked examples, and the files on today’s tools add code you can run yourself. Read them in order as one long history, or jump to any topic that piques your interest.
It’s written for anyone who works with maps or spatial data and wants to know why the tools behave the way they do: GIS analysts, developers, data engineers, students, and anyone who has ever wondered why a shapefile comes in pieces.
The Shape-Files is written by Jacob Hogue.
